subtitle: Us-and-them judgments can be examined honestly without giving up your values, your curiosity or your responsibility to address harm. This course helps you do that work with care.
scope: For staff across DHS. Polarization, Defense and Reversal are concepts from the official IDC, not diagnoses assigned to people here. Private reflection is optional, with practice alternatives and no requirement to enter or share personal accounts. Use no sensitive records in activities. Actual IDI results, conduct concerns and work decisions retain their appropriate processes. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: An us-and-them judgment can make another way of living or working seem automatically worse, or automatically better, before it is understood. This course explores Polarization through personal, community and DHS examples. You will distinguish a meaningful value from a claim of group superiority, recognize idealization, ask more specific questions and preserve responsibility where a harmful action or formal requirement is involved. The aim is a more thoughtful perspective and response, without ranking people or making every disagreement a cultural diagnosis.

intro.heading: Recognize a binary judgment in an account
intro.body:
Polarization is an official IDC concept about opposing group evaluations of cultural difference. The learning question here is whether a practice account ranks groups instead of examining a specific practice, meaning or concern. Disagreement alone does not establish the concept, and a sentence cannot determine a speaker’s IDI result.

Leon values clear start times because they helped organize familiar community activities. Leon says that people using another arrangement have no respect for others. The valued practice and the group judgment are different claims. Leon can explain what timing means to him and examine its actual effect without deciding that everyone associated with another practice has the same character.

A similar shortcut can appear in DHS work. A practice outreach team describes its own channel as inherently superior to another unit’s channel. A task-based comparison would ask which audience, information need and evidence are relevant. Preference and past experience can inform a question, but cannot establish a general ranking of groups.

Begin by separating the value, observable practice and added group evaluation. This makes room for inquiry without requiring you to abandon a meaningful value or treat every proposed action as equally suitable. The task and any actual concern still need evidence and the appropriate responsibility.

items.title: Preference or value
items.body: Leon can value a clear start time and explain its meaning in his own experience. That is not inherently a group-ranking claim. The learning opportunity is to keep the value while examining whether a different arrangement serves another purpose, and whether the actual effect supports a specific concern.

items.title: A superiority claim
items.body: People using another arrangement have no respect assigns character to a group before examining the context. Ask which action and effect Leon observed, rather than accepting the group claim as evidence. A specific concern can remain important after the overgeneralization is removed.

items.title: An inquiry instead of a label
items.body: The facilitator can ask what the timing arrangement needs to accomplish and whose account is missing. Do not declare Leon’s personal placement from the invented statement. A question about the actual practice supports learning without turning the conceptual example into a diagnosis or public ranking.

tabs.label: State a preference
tabs.body: A stated preference identifies what feels meaningful or useful to you. Leon’s preference for clear start times can remain legitimate. It becomes more thoughtful when he distinguishes his experience from what every other person values and examines the actual circumstance rather than treating familiarity as a universal standard.

tabs.label: Rank the groups
tabs.body: Ranking groups makes a specific difference into an inherent superiority claim. It may feel decisive while supplying no evidence about the arrangement. Return to the action, effect and context so a genuine concern can be evaluated without using a group label as the conclusion.

tabs.label: Examine the issue
tabs.body: Examining the issue keeps the value and asks what the practice does in context. The outreach team can compare channels for an actual audience and information need. This supports a qualified choice or question, without assuming all methods are equivalent or diagnosing the person who preferred one.

check.question: Which response to Leon’s practice statement is sound?
check.correct: Separate Leon’s valued timing practice from the group judgment, then examine the actual purpose and effect without assigning an IDI placement.
wrong: Treat the statement as proof of Leon’s assessment result.
Approve the group judgment because the timing value matters to Leon.
Declare every arrangement equally suitable without checking its effect.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response preserves the meaningful value while examining the unsupported group evaluation and actual context.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One statement cannot establish an IDI result. A meaningful value does not validate a group-character judgment. Equal suitability also needs examination rather than assertion. Separate value, action and evaluation, then ask a specific question that keeps the work or personal concern understandable without ranking groups.

intro.heading: Keep belonging without defending superiority
intro.body:
Defense in the official model favors a familiar cultural way through a superiority evaluation. In this course, examine the difference between meaningful attachment and the claim that another group is worse. Valuing a familiar experience does not require that claim. Personal reflection can help you understand the attachment without rejecting your background or ranking someone else’s.

Leon remembers that a clear start time made a neighborhood activity dependable. That memory connects punctuality with care in his experience. He can value the care while noticing that another person may express it differently, or that a different arrangement may need clearer coordination. The memory does not tell him what every person means by respect.

Privately consider a broad familiar value, or use Leon. Ask what the practice meant to you and which generalization you might add when it differs. No answer needs to be entered or shared. A meaningful result may be a clearer distinction between the value and one expression, with the question still open.

This is not a demand to approve every action. If an arrangement caused a specific problem, describe it and seek a suitable response. The aim is to retain a thoughtful relationship with your own experience while examining the other account, rather than treating inquiry as betrayal of belonging.

items.title: Attachment is not the problem
items.body: Leon’s valued memory may offer stability, affection and a sense of belonging. Recognizing another perspective need not remove those meanings. The distinction is between appreciating what the memory gave him and declaring that people with another practice are less caring or less worthy.

items.title: Separate value from expression
items.body: Care may have been expressed through a clear start time in Leon’s remembered setting. He can ask how care might be expressed in a different arrangement without assuming all expressions work equally well. This develops personal meaning while leaving a concrete coordination question available if one exists.

items.title: Private inquiry is sufficient
items.body: A learner can explore the question silently or through Leon’s practice account. No public story, confession or work action is required. Keep the account broad and nonsensitive if anything is shared, and do not use another person’s assumed identity to prove what their practice must mean.

tabs.label: Defend the group ranking
tabs.body: Defending the ranking can make inquiry feel like disloyalty to your own background. The specific value gets attached to a universal claim about people. Separate those claims so you can retain what matters while examining context and effect without turning belonging into superiority.

tabs.label: Reject the familiar entirely
tabs.body: Rejecting the familiar entirely can replace one ranking with another and dismiss meaningful experience. Leon does not need to call his own background inferior to learn. Explore the value and its limits without assuming that openness requires a negative verdict on every familiar practice.

tabs.label: Belonging with inquiry
tabs.body: Belonging with inquiry allows Leon to value dependability and ask what another arrangement means or needs. The question may deepen personal understanding without a workplace product. A specific concern can still be addressed through its actual evidence rather than a general claim about group character.

check.question: Which reflection keeps Leon’s valued experience without a superiority claim?
check.correct: The familiar arrangement made care and dependability meaningful to Leon; he can explore another expression without judging a group as less worthy.
wrong: Meaningful belonging requires believing other groups are inferior.
Learning requires rejecting every familiar value.
The reflection is worthwhile only if it improves a workplace metric.
check.feedbackCorrect: The reflection values personal meaning and opens inquiry without requiring group ranking or instrumental proof.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Belonging does not require declaring another group inferior. Learning need not reject every familiar value. A workplace metric is not required for personal growth. Explore what matters and distinguish it from a universal group claim, privately or through Leon, while retaining any specific issue that needs examination.

intro.heading: Appreciate another account without idealizing it
intro.body:
Reversal is the form of Polarization that idealizes another cultural way while devaluing the familiar one. It can sound generous because the positive judgment is directed outward. Yet a blanket positive claim may still flatten variation, impose a preferred story and skip what the people or practice actually mean.

Leon sees a community event with flexible arrival and notices that participants describe it as welcoming. He concludes that the other group is always more humane and that his familiar arrangements are worthless. The account could instead support a specific appreciation: the event’s welcome practices worked for those participants in that setting. It does not establish a perfect group or a universal rule.

Ask what conditions made the practice useful and which perspectives are still missing. An event can be meaningful while a participant experiences a difficulty not visible to Leon. He can seek appropriate context or consider another public account without requiring someone to correct his worldview through private disclosure.

Appreciation and learning remain valuable. Leon may retain a personal insight about welcome or develop an optional work question. He need not denigrate his background or claim expertise in the other group. A qualified account can recognize a useful practice without treating it as automatically transferable to every situation.

items.title: A favorable stereotype is still a shortcut
items.body: Always more humane assigns a fixed positive quality to a group and may pressure people to fit the learner’s admired image. The claim bypasses their variation and actual experience. Name what the event did well and in which account, instead of using praise as a total explanation of people.

items.title: Do not erase your own account
items.body: Calling the familiar arrangement worthless replaces one broad ranking with another. Leon can value its dependability while appreciating the event’s welcome. A more nuanced reflection holds the specific strengths and questions without requiring that one background be entirely rejected to respect another.

items.title: Transfer needs context
items.body: Flexible arrival may serve this event while a different activity has a fixed responsibility or start requirement. Ask what the practice accomplishes and what conditions support it. Learning from another account does not authorize copying it unchanged or assuming that every participant finds it equally useful.

tabs.label: Idealize the other group
tabs.body: Idealization can turn a specific positive encounter into a universal group claim. Leon may overlook a participant’s difficulty because it contradicts the admired story. Appreciation is more credible when it names the practice, context and account rather than demanding that the group remain a perfect model.

tabs.label: Devalue the familiar group
tabs.body: Devaluing the familiar group keeps an opposing ranking and can dismiss meaningful experience without evidence. Leon can examine a limit in his routine without calling every part worthless. This permits learning and appreciation while retaining a thoughtful rather than contemptuous account of his own background.

tabs.label: Specific appreciation
tabs.body: Specific appreciation names what seemed useful, whose account supports it and what remains to examine. Leon can learn about welcome without claiming group perfection. An optional change still needs its task, context and requirements, so admiration does not become unsupported authority or automatic transfer.

check.question: Which statement appreciates Leon’s practice event without Reversal-style ranking?
check.correct: The described welcome practices seemed useful in this setting; I can examine their context without declaring the other group perfect or my familiar experience worthless.
wrong: The other group is always humane and never has problems.
My familiar group is completely worthless because the event was welcoming.
Any admired practice should replace every existing arrangement without a context check.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement values a specific practice and keeps context, variation and further inquiry open.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A universal positive claim erases variation and possible problems. Dismissing the familiar group maintains a binary ranking. Automatic transfer ignores context and requirements. Appreciate the specific practice and account, examine the conditions and retain meaningful experience without making either group a total verdict.

intro.heading: Preserve ethical responsibility while understanding context
intro.body:
Questioning a group ranking does not mean abandoning ethical judgment or treating harm as a mere style difference. You can respect a person and seek to understand a context while identifying conduct that requires a response. The important distinction is between a supported concern about an action and a total condemnation of a group.

In a practice DHS activity, a participant reports a repeated demeaning remark connected to a protected characteristic. Another person says that avoiding us-and-them thinking means dismissing the concern as a cultural preference. That is not the lesson. The concern needs its appropriate policy and reporting route; optional learning discussion cannot determine the formal finding or become a gate to that route.

A different personal example may concern an invitation that feels pressuring. Leon can name the action and boundary rather than label a whole group coercive. Understanding what the invitation meant does not require accepting pressure or proving the group’s identity caused it. A suitable response addresses the actual situation.

Keep requirements and authority explicit. The UNESCO declaration links cultural diversity with human dignity rather than a blanket approval of conduct. It is a conceptual reference here, not a newly created Minnesota mandate. For actual DHS concerns, use the applicable agency processes and assigned responsibilities, preserving required routes rather than replacing them with a debate about cultural stages.

items.title: Specific concern rather than group verdict
items.body: Describe the repeated remark, its reported context and the appropriate next responsibility. Do not conclude that everyone associated with a group acts that way. Removing the group verdict does not minimize the conduct; it makes the concern more specific and keeps the proper policy process available.

items.title: Understanding is not an excuse
items.body: An explanation of meaning may clarify an interaction without approving it. Leon can understand an invitation’s purpose and still decline a pressuring condition. In DHS work, a cultural explanation cannot substitute for the applicable response to a reported concern or allow optional learning to delay the required route.

items.title: The course makes no finding
items.body: The practice case illustrates a boundary, not a legal or investigative result. Staff need the actual applicable process and responsibilities. The consultant can offer guidance and feedback but is not a new permission gate; actual formal decisions stay with the responsible roles and offices.

tabs.label: Whole-group condemnation
tabs.body: Whole-group condemnation extends a specific concern to people the account does not describe. It can add another inequity and distract from the action needing response. Keep the conduct and evidence specific while using the appropriate route, without treating group character as the formal finding.

tabs.label: Context as blanket excuse
tabs.body: A blanket excuse can make respect for difference sound like a reason to ignore harmful conduct. That confuses understanding with approval. Seek relevant context where appropriate, retain boundaries and use the actual policy process rather than making optional dialogue a condition of a formal response.

tabs.label: Specific concern with proper responsibility
tabs.body: A specific concern identifies the reported action and next responsible process without a group verdict. It allows inquiry and respect while preserving ethical and formal duties. This is a more accountable response than either condemnation of a whole group or reassurance that cultural explanation settles the matter.

check.question: How should the practice reported demeaning remark be handled in this learning example?
check.correct: Keep the concern specific and use the actual appropriate policy/reporting process without group condemnation or making optional dialogue a gate.
wrong: Dismiss the concern as a cultural preference.
Condemn every member of an associated group as the formal outcome.
Require a homemade IDC label before allowing the person to report.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response retains the actual concern and appropriate responsibility while avoiding unsupported group and assessment claims.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A cultural explanation does not automatically dismiss a concern. Whole-group condemnation exceeds the specific account and is not a formal finding. A homemade IDC label cannot gate reporting. Keep the action and evidence specific and preserve the actual process and assigned duties alongside optional learning.

intro.heading: Compare practices using purpose and evidence
intro.body:
Moving away from us-and-them evaluation does not require treating every option as equally effective. It asks for a more specific basis for judgment. Identify the purpose, relevant criteria, evidence and limits. A supported choice about a method is different from saying the people using it are inherently better.

In a practice DHS outreach review, one unit recommends a printed notice and another recommends a digital route. One participant says the familiar unit is always more practical; another says the new route’s team is automatically more enlightened. Both claims skip the audience and actual information need. The review needs evidence about reach, usable information, requirements and resources in the actual setting.

Compare the options without invented numbers or a universal winner. A combined approach or another option may be considered if evidence and responsibility support it. If information is missing, identify the question and appropriate source rather than converting preference into a confident recommendation. No practice comparison establishes an actual service-access outcome.

This practice can also deepen personal thinking. Leon can compare what he values in two activity arrangements without making a group verdict. The inquiry may remain private. A work proposal, however, needs the applicable equity analysis and decision process; this course routine is preparation, not its replacement.

lessons.keyStatement: Compare what the options accomplish rather than the status of their groups.

items.title: Purpose and criteria
items.body: The practice outreach purpose is to provide usable information to the relevant audience. Ask what criteria can examine each route for that purpose, including actual requirements. This is more useful than calling one unit practical or enlightened. Criteria should be explained rather than selected merely to favor the already preferred option.

items.title: Evidence and missing information
items.body: The team needs suitable information about the routes and audience, not imagined statistics. If reach or usability is unexamined, keep it unknown and identify an appropriate source. A group reputation or attractive story cannot stand in for the evidence necessary to support a real recommendation.

items.title: Qualified choice
items.body: A qualified choice explains which criteria and evidence support the option and which limits remain. It may favor one method or a permitted combination. The conclusion concerns the actual task, not the inherent worth of either unit, and actual policy and service decisions use their responsible process.

tabs.label: Favor the familiar
tabs.body: Favoring the familiar may use past success as a total answer to a new audience or need. Past experience can supply a useful question but must fit the current context. Describe what it supports and what remains, rather than treating group reputation as an automatic winning criterion.

tabs.label: Favor the admired
tabs.body: Favoring the admired route may mistake novelty or positive group image for usefulness. The method could still miss an information need or requirement. Ask the same relevant evidence questions across options, without assuming admiration proves either reach or equity in the actual setting.

tabs.label: Purpose-based comparison
tabs.body: A purpose-based comparison examines the audience, criteria, evidence, resources and requirements. It can support a different or combined option without making the groups equal in every respect or ranking their inherent worth. Keep missing information visible and use the actual authorized process before a real recommendation is final.

check.question: What would support the practice outreach comparison?
check.correct: Relevant audience and purpose, explained criteria, suitable evidence and limits, with actual requirements and decision responsibility retained.
wrong: The familiar unit’s status proves its route is always best.
The admired team’s image proves its route is automatically equitable.
Avoid all criteria because choosing a method would rank the people.
check.feedbackCorrect: The comparison judges the method for the actual task without substituting group status for evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Familiar status does not prove universal suitability. An admired image does not establish equity or access. Avoiding criteria prevents a supported choice and confuses evaluating a method with ranking people. Use a clear task basis, identify missing evidence and retain the actual process and responsibility.

intro.heading: Review a more nuanced account without claiming a stage
intro.body:
At the end of the course, ask what the binary judgment has stopped doing for you. Leon may understand that clear timing expresses a meaningful value in his experience without proving other people less caring. He may also appreciate a different welcome practice without idealizing a group. These can be worthwhile personal insights that remain private and unfinished.

The practice outreach team has another possible gain: its comparison now names the audience, criteria and missing evidence rather than ranking units. That is a reasoning improvement. An actual access outcome is still unverified. Do not turn a clearer comparison into proof that the selected route served everyone or that no barriers remain.

Neither result establishes an IDI orientation or guarantees the end of Polarization. The official IDC has five orientations ending with Adaptation. In this program, Integration means the people a process affects help design it; it does not add an official sixth stage. Course answers, disclosure or a successful method comparison do not place a person on the model.

Choose another meaningful inquiry. You can revisit a value privately, use a practice account or examine a work option with suitable evidence and responsibility. Consultant feedback can support knowledge and reflection without doing staff work for them. The aim is continued personal growth and thoughtful practice, not a performance of perfect openness or a ranking of employees.

items.title: A meaningful personal account
items.body: Leon’s account now distinguishes a valued practice from a judgment about other people’s worth. He may keep that understanding private and explore another question later. The insight is valid without an operational metric, public confession or proof that every personal assumption has been found.

items.title: A bounded reasoning gain
items.body: The outreach comparison identifies a purpose and missing evidence. That improves the structure of the practice inquiry but does not establish the actual route’s effectiveness. State what changed and what remains unknown, keeping a real recommendation with the appropriate equity-analysis and decision process.

items.title: A further question rather than a score
items.body: A learner can ask where admiration still substitutes for context or where attachment becomes a universal claim. The question supports another reflection. It does not calculate an assessment result or require private identity disclosure before learning continues; practice examples remain available.

tabs.label: Personal understanding
tabs.body: Personal understanding may become more nuanced as the learner separates value, attachment, appreciation and group ranking. It can remain private or be explored through Leon. A work product is not required for that outcome, and no amount of disclosed detail proves a particular developmental placement.

tabs.label: Work reasoning
tabs.body: Work reasoning can show that a comparison now uses task criteria and evidence questions. That gain remains different from the actual method’s outcome. Keep the scope and missing information visible, rather than declaring complete equity or personal competence because the exercise produced a clearer account.

tabs.label: Continuing growth
tabs.body: Continuing growth leaves space for another personal or work question. A value can matter while its expressions vary; an admired account can teach something while incomplete. Keep inquiry and appropriate responsibility together without a universal guarantee or a hidden cultural score attached to the learner.

check.question: Which review preserves the learning and its limits?
check.correct: Describe a more nuanced personal understanding or task-based reasoning gain, retain open questions and avoid claiming an IDI result from the exercise.
wrong: Declare Polarization permanently eliminated by completing the course.
Score the learner’s orientation from the amount of private detail shared.
Count only measured work improvements as valuable learning.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review recognizes both personal growth and bounded work learning while keeping assessment and evidence limits clear.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Completion does not guarantee every future group judgment is eliminated. Disclosure quantity does not determine an IDI orientation. Personal understanding is valuable without a measured work result. Describe the meaningful or evidence-supported gain and its limits, then choose a further inquiry rather than a personal stage claim.

items.text: Leon separates valued timing from a claim of group inferiority.
The practice review now names relevant comparison criteria.
The actual outreach outcome has not been examined.
Which admired account still needs more context?
Completion guarantees no future binary judgment.
Private detail establishes an official IDC placement.

lessons.next: Value your own experience, appreciate other accounts and keep choices grounded in context rather than group ranking.

scenario.context: Consider this situation: Leon retains a private personal insight and a DHS team improves its comparison questions. A facilitator wants to score everyone’s orientation from these results.
options: Rank personal stages from the exercise results.
Reject Leon’s insight because it has no work metric.
Recognize personal understanding and bounded reasoning, retain questions and keep actual assessment separate.
responses: The exercises do not administer the IDI or establish placement.
Personal cultural growth is valid without operational proof.
This respects the learning paths and their actual limits.

lessons.transfer: Privately name a personal insight or use Leon; optionally describe a work-reasoning gain with its limits and next inquiry.

move.control: You can recognize growth without scoring yourself or another person.
move.failure: A revised account is turned into a personal stage or only work output is valued.
move.next: Keep one meaningful gain and choose another specific question.

jobAid.subtitle: Move from us-and-them judgment toward specific understanding and accountable choices.
remember: Defense and Reversal are official concepts; course examples do not assign personal placement.
A value or appreciation can matter without making a group inherently superior.
Understanding context does not endorse harmful conduct or replace actual duties.

sections.heading: Examine the evaluation
items: Separate your value or preference from an opposing-group claim.
Notice when praise of another group becomes idealization and contempt for the familiar one.
Ask what actual action, meaning or evidence the ranking skips.

sections.heading: Explore meaning and responsibility
items: Reflect privately or use Leon; no entered personal account or work result is required.
Ask appropriate context questions without demanding group representation.
Keep specific concerns and required formal routes available.

sections.heading: Compare and continue
items: For a work option, explain the purpose, criteria, evidence questions and authority.
State supported gains and retain missing information.
Recognize a more nuanced personal account as a valid outcome.
Use consultant guidance for thinking and feedback while carrying out your own practice and work.

sources.title: Intercultural Development Inventory: official IDC overview
sources.note: Explains Polarization, Defense and Reversal within the official five-orientation model. Course activities do not reproduce IDI items or determine a personal assessment result.

sources.title: UNESCO Universal Declaration on Cultural Diversity
sources.note: Article 4 provides a conceptual human-dignity boundary to cultural-diversity claims. The course does not turn the declaration into a new Minnesota operational mandate or make a legal finding.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Conceptual reference for contextual, internally varied cultural accounts, respectful inquiry and reflection. All Leon and outreach cases are newly authored rather than copied activities.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual DHS equity-analysis, training, tools and decision responsibilities remain applicable. Optional comparative exercises are preparation, not a substitute for required review or formal concern processes.
